title: Cindy Crawford 'beyond heartbroken' after death of son Presley at 27
description: Supermodel Cindy Crawford has said she and her family are "beyond heartbroken" over the death of her son Presley Gerber."He is a sweet, beautiful soul
body: Supermodel Cindy Crawford has said she and her family are "beyond heartbroken" over the death of her son Presley Gerber."He is a sweet, beautiful soul who loved and is loved, now and forever," she posted on Instagram, next to a black-and-white photo of him. "We are so proud of how he showed up in the world, with kindness and vulnerability."The 27-year-old died on 20 September at a rehab facility in California. Police said officials are investigating his death as a suspected overdose.Gerber had been a model like his mother and younger sister Kaia, making his catwalk debut for Italian label Moschino aged just 16.Crawford wrote in the post on Sunday: "We feel so blessed to have had Presley in our lives for 27 years.""We are grateful for the outpouring of love and support from so many who know and love our family and even strangers who feel our pain," she also posted."Til we meet again our sweet boy. We love you forever, Mom, Dad and Kaia," she wrote in closing, with an emoji of angel wings.The tribute also listed the dates of his birth and death. The Los Angeles County Medical Examiner lists Gerber's case as pending additional investigation. The Santa Monica Police Department has said there is no indication foul play was involved in his death.Gerber's sister Kaia also dedicated a post to him on Sunday which included a video of the two siblings as children dancing together, a photo of them standing near the ocean, and a four-page letter to "prez" typed out on a blue background.In the letter, she said she had been scared of getting her ears pierced, so "you went first"."But when I held the earring they took from your body, all I could think was: That belongs to you," she wrote. "I am learning how to love you when I cannot see you," she also wrote. "How to tell you something without picking up my phone to call you. How to be your sister in a world that I can't reach for you in," she wrote. In recent years, Gerber had spoken openly about his mental health challenges and drug use and frequently posted videos on Instagram himself for what he called "Mental Health Mondays".His father Rande Gerber, a well-known businessman, co-founded the Casamigos tequila brand with George Clooney.If you're affected by any of the issues in this article you can find details of organisations who can help via the BBC Action Line.Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide, external, external.

title: EU tariffs aimed at China hitting Ukraine, steel boss says
description: The boss of one of Ukraine's biggest steel companies has called on the European Union to drop import restrictions on products made from the country, a
body: The boss of one of Ukraine's biggest steel companies has called on the European Union to drop import restrictions on products made from the country, arguing it has been "bundled together" in measures aimed a curbing cheap imports from the likes of China.Yuriy Ryzhenkov, chief executive of Metinvest, told the BBC the recently-imposed tariffs on imported steel to the EU were "unfair" and had been put in place "without any consideration for the situation Ukraine is in".He said he wished to see "at least a carve out" for Ukraine to access the EU market.A spokesperson for the European Commission said the EU "took into account the difficult situation" of Ukraine when deciding its steel policy.The trading bloc has recently imposed restrictions on steel imports in an effort to protect steel manufacturers of member nations.It has capped the amount of steel which can enter the EU tax free at 18.3 million tonnes per year - a 47% reduction from 2024 levels.There are some country-specific quotas in the policy, but the overall aim is to cut the amount of steel that can be imported due to member nations struggling to compete with cheap imports from the likes of China and Turkey.Despite a free-trade agreement (FTA) being in place between the EU and Ukraine, the FTA does not stop the EU from introducing separate trade protection measures."Ukraine has been bundled together into those measures without any consideration for the situation Ukraine is in," Ryzhenkov said, pointing to the war with Russia."Access to the European market is crucial for survival," he added. "The restrictive measures that have been put in place by the authorities in the European Union, they don't help."I think it's unfair that Ukraine has been treated in the same way as all of the other importers into the European Union."The Ukraine steel industry estimates steel exports to the EU could ultimately fall by about 50–60%.The EU said Ukraine's specific steel quota guaranteed exports of the metal, but acknowledged this was at a "level lower than in the past years"."Despite the war effort, Ukraine remains an important exporter of steel to the EU," a spokesperson said, adding it had "offered compensations" to its largest suppliers, which included Ukraine.Steel products are a foundation in Ukraine's economy. Before the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, metallurgy and mining accounted for roughly 10% of Ukraine's national income and a third of its exports. The EU is its top customer.But the industry has suffered from the continued Russian bombardment.All of Ukraine's steel mills have been bombed at points since the conflict began in 2022, but Ryzhenkov said strikes had "intensified significantly recently".At one point in September, there was "no single tonne of steel produced" in Ukraine for the first time in about 150 years, he added.Almost 800 Metinvest workers have been killed since the war began.Ryzhenkov said the company had "improved the covered areas" at its mills where workers can shelter during air raids."The only thing we can do is to design procedures to keep people safe and just obey those procedures and try to minimise the risks.""Unfortunately, you cannot cover a whole steel mill to avoid it being damaged."Ryzhenkov said he expected the coming winter to be "one of the hardest in our history"."We are in a dire situation when we don't have logistics to access any other market apart from the EU and cutting our available market by 60%, that doesn't help for the industry to survive."

schema.headline: EU tariffs aimed at China hitting Ukraine, steel boss says

title: Trump says suspension of Russia sanctions is to keep peace negotiations going
description: US President Donald Trump has said his decision to suspend several Russian sanctions is an effort to keep Moscow at the negotiating table."I am in the
body: US President Donald Trump has said his decision to suspend several Russian sanctions is an effort to keep Moscow at the negotiating table."I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine," Trump said on his Truth Social messaging platform, adding that he didn't want to "do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table".Trump blocked numerous sanctions on Russia on Friday night, two days before they were due to take effect, as a row with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky deepened.Zelensky told NBC News on Sunday that siding with Russian President Vladimir Putin would be a "historic mistake".Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev has responded to Trump's order by calling it "an important and truly historic moment". He said the sanctions, which were passed by the US Congress and signed into law by the US president in September, would have inflicted "serious damage" on the US and global market.US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has described the suspension of the sanctions as a 60-day pause during which their potential impact on the US and global economies would be analysed.In his Truth Social post, Trump also said Zelensky "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did", adding "he could have made a better deal two years ago than he can now".Zelensky has pushed for an end to fighting, and has repeatedly said that Putin doesn't want peace, since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.Relations between Washington and Kyiv frayed after the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel last week.Despite the international sanctions, Russia has still been able to export oil, much of it to China and India - often at attractive discounts. According to the think-tank Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), China has taken about half of Russia's crude exports, with India accounting for about 37%.In remarks to a European Union summit, after Trump announced the deal to buy diesel from Russia and said Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with" than Putin, Zelensky said it was nice to be among "real leaders".Zelensky has repeatedly pushed for stringent sanctions to limit funding that Russia can use in its war effort. After the latest move from the US, however, he said he believed the Trump administration would lift more sanctions against Russia.Ukraine and its European allies criticised Trump's plans to import Russian diesel to help lower US energy prices, which have skyrocketed during the Iran war.The deal, according to Zelensky, was tantamount to the US investing in Russia's war effort.Concerns that Trump is siding with Russia have been heightened by disruption to Starlink, a US-provided satellite system used by Ukraine. That hampered Kyiv's ability to protect itself from Russian attacks.Zelensky said US officials had linked speed restrictions to technical issues.However, he said Ukraine had tested Starlink on EU territory and found it was operating at higher speeds.Trump has denied both deliberately slowing down the network and a further accusation from Zelensky that the US had stopped sharing defence intelligence.

schema.headline: Trump says suspension of Russia sanctions is to keep peace negotiations going

title: Four killed, dozens injured in major fire at Canada military base
description: Four members of the Canadian military have died and dozens were injured in a major fire at a base in the province of Alberta.Addressing the nation on
body: Four members of the Canadian military have died and dozens were injured in a major fire at a base in the province of Alberta.Addressing the nation on Sunday from Ottawa, Prime Minister Mark Carney described it as "one of the worst tragedies for the forces on Canadian soil in peacetime".The fire broke out at about 16:00 local time (22:00 GMT) on Saturday at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, one of the country's busiest military training bases, and is now contained. Its cause is still unclear, but officials said it did not appear tied to "terrorist activity". "The nation is in mourning for those brave members of our armed forces who we have lost," said Carney. The BBC has confirmed that Sgt Morgan Wong, Pte Shaun Farrell, Pte Aidan Goulding and Pte Hayden Lykkemark have died.Of the 39 injured people being cared for in hospital, at least 19 are in a critical condition, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said at a press briefing on Sunday evening.Fire and rescue teams are remaining at the scene to contain any potential flare-ups, Wainwright Mayor Bruce Pugh told the BBC.Members of the infantry had been conducting "high-intensity combat training with live munitions" at a grenade range and attack range, where 10 soldiers practise attacking a simulated enemy, Maj-Gen Wade Rutland told reporters at the briefing. "There was a multitude of ordnance moving through the Wainwright training area," he said, including a grenade launcher, grenades, small arms and ammunition.A grass fire ignited about 1km (0.6 miles) away, with the cause currently under investigation, and moved toward the attack range."What I would say is there was multiple training activities happening throughout the training area at the time," he  said. "Uncommonly strong winds caused the fire to spread rapidly and shift direction towards the range administrative area."Cannon fire had been heard coming from the base on Saturday before it suddenly stopped, Mayor Pugh told the BBC, noting it's not uncommon to hear cannons being fired there.News then came through that local emergency services had been deployed to an "all hands on deck" situation.Carney said military and emergency crews fought the flames throughout the night in "some of the worst conditions imaginable". The people who were hurt were on the attack range and included reservists and soldiers from the Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry, officials said.In a statement early on Sunday, the Canadian Armed Forces said that "while the incident remains under investigation, at this time, there are no indications that it was the result of any terrorist activity". Rutland told the briefing: "We do not believe this [incident] to be a result of any oil and gas infrastructure nor any outside interference".Wainwright, about 210km (130 miles) east of Edmonton, Alberta's capital, is one of the main bases used by the Canadian military for live-fire training exercises, and it houses troops from Canada and allied countries. About 690 military personnel and 300 civilian workers are on site on a typical day.Warren Thirsk, an emergency department doctor at the Royal Alexandra Hospital, told broadcaster CBC that the number of patients involved in the incident had "completely overwhelmed" healthcare facilities in Wainwright.The Royal Alexandra Hospital is in Edmonton, where patients are being transferred. The hospital at first declared a code orange - a disaster-response protocol for a high-casualty incident. That has since been stood down. The provincial health agency said in a statement on Sunday that it deployed 30 units directly into Wainwright, including 22 ground ambulances, six fixed-wing and two rotary wing units. "It is anticipated that care for patients impacted by this incident will be intensive and will add to existing high demand on acute care in Alberta," it said, adding that patients were being treated at facilities across the province. STARS, the regional air ambulance service, said aircraft and crews from Edmonton, Saskatoon, and Calgary had been deployed. Brandon Simmons, who lives in long-term care at the Wainwright Health Centre, told Reuters that when code orange was announced, nurses dropped everything and immediately started grabbing stretchers, gurneys and medical equipment before running to the front entrance.Ambulances kept coming "throughout the night", he said."I heard people screaming inside of those vehicles that will never end up being out of my mind," he recalled, saying it was "like a scene from a war movie".Additional reporting by Lisa Lambert

schema.headline: Four killed, dozens injured in major fire at Canada military base

title: Inside the shadowy world of anti-Putin sabotage from within Russia
description: Two Russian men secretly working for Ukraine's intelligence services have given rare accounts of operations they claim to have been involved with, tha
body: Two Russian men secretly working for Ukraine's intelligence services have given rare accounts of operations they claim to have been involved with, that have targeted military assets and personnel inside Russia.One of the men, whom we are calling Ivan, claims to have played a role from Russia in Ukrainian drone attacks on strategic bombers and munitions factories on his home soil.He features in a BBC World Service documentary about the shadowy world of Russian saboteurs.The documentary, by independent Polish journalist Marcin Mamon, also features a man we are calling Foma, a Russian living in exile in Poland. Foma runs a network of undercover volunteers in Russia, that surveils high-level officers that the GUR - Ukraine's military intelligence service - is considering targeting, he says. He stresses they are never involved in the attacks themselves.He was also tight-lipped about who they were surveilling, but after Lt Gen Fanil Sarvarov was assassinated in December last year in Moscow, Foma admitted he had provided the Ukrainians with intelligence on him.There have been previous media reports of Russian sabotage groups, but it is rare to get access to someone operating on the ground, like Ivan, explaining alleged activities.The GUR has confirmed that Ivan and Foma are both working for the agency. But it also has acknowledged that it cannot know the full picture. When Ivan's handler was pressed on whether he could be trusted, the handler replied: "I'm not sure of anyone, except myself."And both the GUR and the men are cautious about how much detail they share, making it impossible to verify the activities the men claim to have carried out.The broad tactics Ivan and Foma describe, however, have been acknowledged by the Ukrainian authorities. Kyiv has spoken of its strategy of co-ordinated drone attacks  on what it claims are legitimate targets inside Russia, and has acknowledged it uses secret agents for this.There have also been several political assassinations in Russia since the start of the war. As a matter of policy, Ukraine never officially admits or claims responsibility for targeted attacks, though a Ukrainian intelligence officer has previously admitted to the BBC it was behind the killing of senior military figure Lt Gen Igor Kirillov in December 2024. It is difficult to confirm how many Russians are doing this kind of work for Ukraine. According to Foma, they number about 300-500, though this is impossible to verify.If you are outside the UK, watch on YouTube, external and listen to the BBC World Service Documentary Podcast - Shadowmen: Russians working with UkraineIvan and Foma say they are both opposed not just to Russia's war in Ukraine, but to President Vladimir Putin's regime - and believe his political future depends on the war's outcome."At the moment... I think the [Putin] regime might fall if they lose the war… Through our actions... we are trying to speed this up," Ivan says.His work, he told Mamon, involved surveilling military sites, and locating places to hide drone components, in preparation for potential attacks on Russian assets."When these [drone] components are combined… it turns out a formidable weapon, which with a single blow can destroy an object that costs many, many millions of dollars," Ivan said.He sent Mamon a video which showed him apparently hiding explosives near a Russian military airfield.If he had been caught, he would have been charged with terrorism, and jailed for decades.Foma's work is different - he operates remotely, training his volunteers in Russia, online. Mamon watched him conducting one such tutorial - on how to trail a senior military official marked for surveillance."You will get a file... from me or a colleague… with the proposed target. The file will contain [the target's] photo, his data, his details, date of birth, age, and a description of him. There'll be information on his car, if he has one. When you go to the target, don't take a phone," he told his volunteers.Foma was once part of the Russian elite, so he claims to have a unique set of contacts and constant flow of insider information.He showed Mamon on his laptop how he mapped military targets."This shows a database... the location of storage warehouses, and military units. Where generals live… Where the pilots of strategic bombers who shell Ukraine live."In order to break the system, you need to understand how it works. Then you can aim for their weak points."He said there were about "three dozen" people in his network split between Russia, Ukraine and elsewhere in Europe, with the contingent outside Russia providing logistical support, such as tracking targets' digital footprints.Foma stressed that the GUR suggests the targets to be surveilled, but that he and his team check for themselves that these individuals should be considered military criminals."As a rule… we also check the data [on that person]… Only after that we say whether we work or not."But he argued that his team's actions were justified."I want people who do terrible things on behalf of Putin and Russia in Ukraine… to understand that they'll have to pay for it. I want them to get scared."Foma stressed that he only passed on intelligence to the Ukrainians, and his network did not carry out any assassinations themselves.Of the assassination of Gen Sarvarov, killed in December 2025, he later texted Mamon to say: "Keeping track of him took quite an effort. He lived alternately with his mistress and his colleague. Covered his tracks and constantly changed his schedule."But Foma did not share any plans with Mamon and the BBC in advance.Ivan, however, was tight-lipped about the work he had been involved with, even after the event.Foma did his own digging on Ivan.After checking with his military intelligence contacts in both Ukraine and Russia, he thought it likely that Ivan had been involved in a plan to strike Russia's largest military drone factory at Yelabuga in June last year, external. One person was reported to have been killed in the incident. Ivan stressed that the aim is always to try to avoid harming civilians.Operations have clearly been risky for Ivan too."The most serious case was when my car was stopped for inspection and I had the handmade explosives on me. The risk was very high - however as you can see, I was not detected," he said.To mitigate the risk of being compromised, "there is no clear structure" to the work, he said, adding he had never met and did not know the identity of others he had been working alongside.Foma has the same rule for his operatives."As soon as you start gathering people in groups, in general chats… leaving a mark on the internet, with a high probability this whole group will be quickly detained or destroyed," he said.Ivan stressed there were few people left in Russia suitable for this kind of work."Most of the ideological people have either left the country or are already behind bars," he said.Many Russians involved in sabotage work on their native soil are therefore either oblivious - for example lorry drivers unaware that their cargoes have been compromised - or are individuals who have been paid, the BBC understands.Ivan, on the other hand, says he is doing this work for ideological reasons - he used to be a member of the political opposition. As such, his movements would be expected to be monitored closely by the Russian authorities.So it was a surprise that he managed to frequently leave Russia and return.Mamon persuaded Ivan to drive him into the Georgian desert, where they could speak freely - and asked him how the Ukrainians could trust him."You go to a third country… where [Ukraine's] agents meet you… and conduct lie detector tests," Ivan told him.Mamon asked Ivan to put him in touch with one of his GUR handlers in Ukraine. This man immediately rang Ivan on speaker phone - apparently demonstrating that Ivan worked for him. They spoke in code, referring to "repairs at the school".But later, the handler admitted he could not rule out the possibility Ivan might work for the Russians too, either voluntarily or under duress.Foma thinks the fact that Ivan can travel freely does not necessarily constitute a red flag."There are all sorts of holes in [the country's governance], and if you know them, or are just lucky, then you can jump through the holes… and live in the system. Like a mouse in a piece of cheese," he told Mamon.Perhaps more compellingly, if Ivan had also been spying for FSB, it would seem likely that he would share what he knew of Ukraine's attack plans with the Russian agency. More than a year before a devastating strike by more than 100 Ukrainian drones, Ivan had been telling Marcin there would be a major attack on strategic bombers on military airfields across Russia, though he never said when or where.Marcin asked Ivan how he coped with the work."Fear is always present," he said. "It follows me everywhere. Even if you don't do anything, you're still afraid. This is Russia."But he was optimistic that eventually his life would change."Putin won't live forever," he said.

schema.headline: Inside the shadowy world of anti-Putin sabotage from within Russia

title: Macron calls for calm in France and warns rioting must not escalate
description: Macron calls for 'calm and order' after riots across FranceFigure caption, Watch: James Waterhouse speaks to looted shop owners on the streets of Pari
body: Macron calls for 'calm and order' after riots across FranceFigure caption, Watch: James Waterhouse speaks to looted shop owners on the streets of ParisByJack BurgessFrench President Emmanuel Macron has called for "calm and order" after a major day of protests turned into rioting and looting on Saturday, and as some disorder continued in Paris on Sunday.In a national address from the Élysée Palace, he warned those who had taken part not to "escalate", adding: "We all feel anger and shame."Some 550,000 demonstrators took to the streets for largely peaceful protests against rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools.Macron said a distinction must be drawn between the "legitimate demands" of protesters and "those who destroyed, smashed and looted". Police have arrested about 2,400 people, according to France's interior ministry.The French president said "nothing justifies" the "unbridled" violence seen and said those involved would face justice.Groups of rioters, some dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas, also came out in Paris, Marseille and other towns and cities, with some setting fire to cars and buildings.Figure caption, 'Very upsetting': Residents in shock after historic French town hall set alightOn Sunday, looting and clashes with police continued on a smaller scale in parts of the capital and Lyon.Tear gas and stun grenades were fired at hundreds of people in Paris, according to the AFP news agency, and bottles and rocks were again hurled at police. Sunday saw cities across the country confront the impact of what developed into one of the worst bouts of disorder in modern French history.In Limoges, the ornate 19th Century city hall was gutted by a fire started by rioters on Saturday, its clock tower and roof collapsing and the flames took hold.Image source, Mairie de LimogeImage caption, A view of the damage inside Limoges town hall on Sunday morningSpeaking near the ruined building, Annèyse said: "This is very upsetting. Harming heritage buildings just because you are angry at the government is selfish, I think. It's hurting everybody.""It's awful and unbelievable," said another man who gave his name as Gerrard. "We are very sad and I think it will be a long time to put it back as it was before."Shopkeepers were seen early on Sunday morning picking up large shards of glass in Paris as rubbish trucks cleared up debris on some of the larger streets.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Fires were lit and shops looted during smaller scale disorder in Paris on SundayWidespread looting took place across the cities of Paris, Marseille and Lille, as well as other areas.Macron said local prefects and mayors would draft measures to protect shops and civic buildings.The president also said there would be "full transparency" over the police response to the demonstrations.Tear gas and water cannon were turned on crowds over the weekend and riot police were seen hitting people with batons in several places.France's interior ministry said about 1,000 police officers were injured on Saturday, seven of them seriously.Image source, ReutersImage caption, A man tries to extinguish a fire in Paris on SundayStudent protests which began last month escalated significant on Saturday after they were joined by trade union members and other anti-government groups.The response from political figures has pointed to France's deep political divisions as the country prepares for an election in April which could see the hard-right pitted against the hard-left.France's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said that while demonstrating was a fundamental right, there were "outrages" committed by "several thousand far-left individuals" who were determined to target public buildings and confront the police.Later, they were joined by "delinquents who looted and ransacked numerous businesses in several cities in France", he said.Jean-Luc Mélenchon - leader of the hard-left La France Insoumise party - heavily criticised Nuñez and police chiefs on social media. He said they had "shown complete incompetence" with their handling of the demonstrations and called them "specialists in organised chaos".Meanwhile, the leader of the hard-right National Rally party, Marine Le Pen, condemned the "exploitation" of anger "by political forces that encourage violence".

schema.headline: Macron calls for calm in France and warns rioting must not escalate

title: People playing loud music on buses could face £100 fine
description: Passengers who play loud music on buses in England could be fined up to £100 under an attempt by the government to crack down on antisocial behaviour.
body: Passengers who play loud music on buses in England could be fined up to £100 under an attempt by the government to crack down on antisocial behaviour.The measures also seek to tackle littering, vaping and threatening behaviour to help improve journeys on all forms of public transport.Offenders on buses could be issued with the fines under new powers for local authorities.A national campaign asking rail passengers "share the carriage, not the noise" is also being launched. The proposed crackdown has been welcomed by campaigners, but some have questioned how it can be enforced."We've all been on the train when someone starts blasting music or videos from their phone. It gets on your nerves and can quickly spoil the journey," said Prime Minister Andy Burnham.Under existing powers, those who are asked to stop and refuse could be removed from a train or fined up to £1,000. The phenomenon has been given many terms - including loudcasting or sodcasting - and in recent years, Ofcom, YouGov and Transport for London (TfL) have all published polls showing the vast majority of people dislike it.Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said small changes in behaviour "can make a massive difference to people's experience on public transport".The government said it had issued new guidance to local authorities on powers - which were introduced earlier this year - to help them crackdown on loud music and other antisocial behaviour on buses in England.These new powers allow them to impose new rules on buses, but still need to be signed off by the Transport SecretaryThose who commit offences could face fixed penalties of up to £100.The government says bus drivers will not be responsible for enforcing the new rules. It says authorised officers, including Transport Safety Officers and the Police, will  deal with the incidents.Meanwhile a new national campaign aims to remind rail passengers to "share the carriage, not the noise", to improve journeys for everyoneThe campaign will be launched across operator websites, social media, and in carriages. The government said this would end the current "patchwork" of approaches across different rail operators, and help create "a clear, consistent message across the network".The general secretary of the TSSA transport union, Maryam Eslamdoust, said tackling antisocial behaviour on public transport was "a step in the right direction".However, she added that the government must also "urgently confront the violence, threats and abuse faced by passengers and transport workers"."Increasing the budget for British Transport Police is vital to protect people, respond to incidents and bring violent offenders to justice," she said.Michael Solomon Williams from the Campaign for Better Transport told the BBC antisocial behaviour could be a "real deterrent" to people using public transport, especially those with  different accessibility needs.He also questioned how the new measures will be enforced. "When local authorities are required to do the enforcement there are perhaps some question marks about how a local police force might be called upon on bus services, for example, where we don't tend to see British Transport Police."Richard Holden MP, Shadow Transport Secretary, said: "After we led the charge against antisocial behaviour on public transport last summer, Ministers have worked out that nobody wants to endure pounding techno or blaring hip hop on a packed train or bus."But passengers and railway staff face far more serious problems. Assaults against rail staff have risen by 68%, while prosecutions have slumped under Labour. It's time for Andy Burnham to get serious about enforcement, tackling violence and protecting those who work on our railways."Liberal Democrat Transport spokesperson, Olly Glover MP said: "Tough talk means nothing without enforcement."Unless the Government funds transport safety officers on the ground, these new rules won't be worth the paper they're printed on."Independent watchdog Transport Focus said research it had published in June showed personal safety and security was now fundamental to passengers' confidence in the railway."Four in 10 passengers say that anti-social behaviour has made them feel vulnerable when travelling," said Alex Campbell, Transport Focus's director of policy and insight."Measures that reduce nuisance behaviour, such as playing loud music and vaping, can help improve people's experience and encourage more people to choose public transport."

schema.headline: People playing loud music on buses could face £100 fine

title: North Korea: What satellite images reveal about Kim Jong Un's summer retreat
description: Photos show luxury boat with 50m pool and water slides near Kim Jong Un's summer retreatImage source, Vantor/BBCBySoram CheonBBC Korean and Aghnia Adz
body: Photos show luxury boat with 50m pool and water slides near Kim Jong Un's summer retreatImage source, Vantor/BBCBySoram CheonBBC Korean and Aghnia AdzkiaEast Asia Visual JournalismAn 80m (263ft) luxury vessel has been repeatedly spotted in satellite images off North Korea's Wonsan coast from July to mid-October this year. What stands out is the 50m swimming pool along the deck, with a cluster of waterslides at one end.After sitting idle for months at a maintenance facility, it relocated in early July to waters off a strip of coastline known as the Kalma Peninsula. This is close to Wonsan, a seaside resort with a sprawling villa used by North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and his family.It was not the only large vessel on the move. A handful of others were also repeatedly seen near Kim's villa, in satellite images analysed by the BBC.The vessels are widely believed to be used by Kim and his family. Former North Korean officials, defectors and experts say it would be difficult for anyone unconnected to the regime's leadership to own or freely use vessels of this size."In winter, they would keep them at the shipyard. When summer came, they would bring them out and move them to Kim Jong Un's villa or towards Kalma, and use them for swimming and recreation," says Ri Jong Ho. Ri was once an official at the Workers' Party's Office 39, which is believed to be involved in raising and managing foreign currency for the leadership.The wealth of those who sit at the top of the secretive North Korean dictatorship is just as hard to pin down as the country's economic figures. The United Nations and others rely on estimates to classify North Korea as one of the world's poorest countries, with an especially large military budget that funds a sanctioned nuclear programme.Most North Koreans, according to a 2025 UN report, live under "systematic, widespread and gross human rights violations" with total state control, widespread forced labour and chronic food shortages that leave an estimated 40% of the population undernourished.But the regime has long been known to live in luxury. We don't know the cost of the vessels seen in the satellite imagery, but comparable luxury yachts run from tens of millions to over $100m (£75m). Kim's much smaller, 29-metre Princess yacht was previously estimated to be worth about $7m.While vessel locations alone cannot definitively establish the family's whereabouts, their movements - which overlap with gaps in Kim's public appearances - point to activities that would otherwise remain out of public view.Wonsan is where Kim Jong Un spent part of his childhood with his mother, according to biographers and intelligence reports, and one expert told the BBC the city has been associated with the family since his father Kim Jong Il's rule.A defector who served for 13 years guarding residences used by then leader Kim Jong Il - through the 1990s to the early 2000s - told the BBC the villas around Wonsan were used as a retreat by the elite. He recalls seeing dozens of children and teens waterskiing during summer.North Korean state media rarely publishes reports about Kim being on holiday, instead framing such visits as official inspections or guidance. But defectors interviewed by the BBC appeared to be aware that the family spent holidays in Wonsan, suggesting that at least some North Koreans knew about it.North Korean state media also claims Wonsan is home to high-rise hotels, restaurants, shops, sports facilities and water parks, and can accommodate nearly 20,000 visitors.State media and Russian outlets have published images of small groups of Russian tourists visiting the Wonsan Kalma resort, which opened in July 2025. Although developed to attract foreign visitors, the resort is also open to local tourists.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, North Korean tourists on a beach in KalmaA South Korean news report, citing an unnamed source, says some locals were offered four-night tour packages for around $100, a substantial sum for most North Koreans. The country's per capita GDP - around $667 in 2024, according to the UN - is a small fraction of South Korea's $36,227.For the majority of North Koreans, holidays are out of reach. And while a growing middle class does exist, they might not have much time for leisure.Defectors told the BBC that workers, office employees and cooperative farmers are legally entitled to 14 days of annual leave, but this is rarely followed.Taking consecutive days off to travel is unusual. People typically take weekend trips or travel during national holidays instead of designated "summer holidays".Even if leave is granted, travel itself is restricted, with official permission required for people to travel outside their city or county. Moving freely is sometimes as much a luxury as the holiday itself.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Ordinary North Koreans struggle to earn a decent living  The BBC tracked four large vessels around Wonsan, measuring approximately 50m, 55m, 60m and 80m. All four vessels repeatedly appeared around Kim's Wonsan villa this year.The largest vessel showed the clearest activity, moving from the dock to the waters off the Kalma Peninsula, where it has been since July.Two of the other vessels - 50m and 55m - were repeatedly seen until the end of August around Tae and Sin islands, close to Wonsan.Satellite images also showed four smaller boats alongside the 50m vessel.Image source, VantorImage caption, The 50m vessel was seen in waters near Tae island on 4 July 2026.Satellite imagery expert Jeong Seong-hak said the smaller boats ferried people, fuel and supplies to the larger vessel, adding that small islands like Tae and Sin offered "secluded maritime retreats where privacy can be maintained away from public view".The 60m vessel was repeatedly seen near Kim's Wonsan villa until as recently as last week.Though North Korea has never publicly disclosed the vessels' official ownership, BBC's analysis of historical satellite imagery found a large vessel with the same distinctive characteristics in Wonsan in 2002, when Kim Jong Il ruled North Korea.Former NBA star Dennis Rodman, who visited the North in 2013, told the Sun that he had spent much of his seven-day visit with Kim Jong Un around Wonsan, where they went jet-skiing and horse riding.He also described a 60m vessel they used as a cross between a ferry and a Disney boat. It is unclear if this is the same 60m boat pictured in the above satellite imagery.To most North Koreans, the life lived by the Kims and others who support the regime would seem not just extravagant but unimaginable. Especially because state propaganda is dedicated to presenting the "supreme leader" as a selfless man who always puts the nation first."Kim Jong Un is supposed to be a 'leader of the people'," Ri Jong Ho says, "yet he has four luxury vessels like these while ordinary people are struggling just to get one meal a day."Graphics by: Arvin Supriyadi

schema.headline: North Korea: What satellite images reveal about Kim Jong Un's summer retreat

title: Burnham warns of Neets-fuelled 'economic catastrophe and moral failure'
description: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has warned the UK faces an "economic catastrophe and moral failure" due to the nearly one million young people not in educ
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has warned the UK faces an "economic catastrophe and moral failure" due to the nearly one million young people not in education, employment or training.Writing in the Times newspaper, external, Burnham has laid out his case for the government to "invest in the success of our young people" rather than "pay for failure through the benefits system"."Benefits will become the backstop, not the starting point," Burnham wrote in his piece published in Monday's paper.Later this week, the government is expected to announce plans to give young people thousands of job opportunities. The Conservative Party has labelled the government's youth employment strategy "a disaster".According to the latest data from the Office for National Statistics, there are almost a million people aged 16 to 24 known as Neets - not in education, employment or training.In his opinion column, the prime minister said this reflected a "generation being denied its chance to get on in life"."This is an economic catastrophe and a moral failure. And it must change," he wrote.Burnham said two years of Covid lockdowns, social media that erodes "confidence and sense of belonging", an education system focused on the "university route", job markets with "too few opportunities" and failures of previous governments have all contributed to the Neets crisis."Today, the welfare system provides an assessment, a payment and, after that, goodbye," Burnham wrote. "Too often there is no support, no offer of skills and no opportunity to get a job."He flagged a shift in the approach to welfare, which he said "will no longer begin by establishing which benefits a young person is entitled to" but rather "begin with their ambitions and the help they need to achieve them".The prime minister added: "The safety net will always be there for those who cannot work. But if someone can work with the right help, the government has a duty to do everything in its power to make that happen."Ministers are this week set to release plans for tens of thousands of new youth apprenticeships and placements in the construction industry, and at accounting, consulting and legal firms.Shadow Business and Trade Secretary Julia Lopez said: "Labour have been a disaster for youth jobs. Their tax hikes and red tape have made it harder for businesses to hire, invest and grow, destroying opportunities for young people looking to take their first step on the career ladder."Burnham confirmed the long-awaited full review of young people and work will be published next month, and vowed to take its recommendations "seriously".The review's author, former health secretary Alan Milburn, has argued for the need to "redistribute money from the welfare system to more employment support" in an interview with the Guardian, external published on Sunday."This is not a workshy, snowflake generation," Milburn said. "If we provide more opportunities and we provide more support, the overwhelming majority of young people will take that, because that's what they want. The system isn't delivering what young people want, which is a job."Milburn calculated that the government spends 25 times more on benefits for young people than getting them into work, describing the current rate of Neets as "shameful".Chancellor John Healey, who is due to hand down his first budget on 28 October, told the Labour party conference in September the government had a "moral duty" to address welfare spending.

schema.headline: Burnham warns of Neets-fuelled 'economic catastrophe and moral failure'

title: Home sellers cut asking prices on 3,000 properties a day, says Rightmove
description: Sellers who have contacted the BBC's Your Voice have pointed to the difficulties created by lots of homes on the market, and extra problems for those
body: Sellers who have contacted the BBC's Your Voice have pointed to the difficulties created by lots of homes on the market, and extra problems for those selling leasehold properties in England.One, who was selling his late father's home in south Wales, said: "The market is dead. Lots for sale; no-one buying. No-one thinks it's going to get easier." Tarah Lourens, chief operating officer at Rightmove, said that "emotional" factors influenced sellers pricing a home - as they "put a value on the time and money they have invested in their home".But she said that buyers simply considered everything they could buy at their budget.Agents said that valuations now drew on huge amounts of data. Craig Webster, of Tiger Sales and Lettings in Blackpool, said that getting an initial price correct when new to the market was crucial."That's when you have the greatest opportunity to capture the attention of active buyers," he said.Katie Griffin, from surveyors Sawdye and Harris in Devon, said that having to correct a price could ultimately lead to a seller accepting less than even a revised asking price."The property may already have been online for several months and buyers can start asking why it has not sold," she said.But Andrew Boast, chief executive of SAM Conveyancing, said sellers might still not be losing out, if they had negotiated aggressively when buying the home and had seen it rise in value while they owned it.

schema.headline: Home sellers cut asking prices on 3,000 properties a day, says Rightmove

title: Suspects hunted after police officer injured in shooting in Nottingham city centre
description: Neghat Khan, leader of Nottingham City Council, said she was "deeply shocked and saddened" by news of the shooting. "My thoughts and full support are
body: Neghat Khan, leader of Nottingham City Council, said she was "deeply shocked and saddened" by news of the shooting. "My thoughts and full support are with the injured police officer, their family, and their colleagues across Nottinghamshire Police," she added.​"Nottingham City Council is working tirelessly alongside the police to support the investigation and ensure those responsible are swiftly caught and brought to justice.​"While incidents of this nature are extremely rare, our commitment to keeping Nottingham safe is absolute. "Thanks to the daily bravery of our police and community protection officers, Nottingham remains a safe city, and residents can be assured that every available resource is being deployed."In a post on social media, Nadia Whittome, MP for Nottingham East, encouraged anyone with information to contact the police. "My thoughts are with the injured police officer and his family following this truly shocking incident," she wrote. "We all wish him a full and speedy recovery."

schema.headline: Suspects hunted after police officer injured in shooting in Nottingham city centre

title: GTA 6: Can you cheat on someone with a video game character?
description: Image source, Rockstar gamesImage caption, The relationship between the two main characters, Jason and Lucia, is at the centre of Rockstar's latest Gr
body: Image source, Rockstar gamesImage caption, The relationship between the two main characters, Jason and Lucia, is at the centre of Rockstar's latest Grand Theft Auto titleByJim ReedHealth reporterImagine your partner spending hours flirting with someone else, trying to hold their hand and taking them on dates. Most people would have questions.But what if that someone only exists inside a video game?The latest instalment in Rockstar's blockbuster Grand Theft Auto franchise is set to be the biggest entertainment launch of the year when it is released next month.Judging by previews, the connection between its two main characters is a central feature.Rockstar has hinted that the Bonnie and Clyde-type protagonists Jason and Lucia do not have to become a full-on romantic couple.But their relationship can grow by spending time together outside of the main crime and life-on-the-run storyline – through shopping, visiting bars and restaurants and working out together.Smaller interactions like holding hands and quickly responding to each other's texts can help build a bond.The idea has restarted a debate almost as old as gaming itself: if you are that invested in a fictional relationship, is your real-life partner entitled to be upset?In September, polling company YouGov put that question to more than 4,000 British adults.About 6% said they would regard it as cheating, while a further 19% said they would "not be okay with it". Women were considerably more likely than men to take a dim view.Alli Franco, a 30-year-old Texan who posts anime and gaming content to more than a million followers, external on TikTok, says she felt "dismayed" watching the debate unfold online."If your partner is insecure about a fictional character, then there needs to be some serious reflection," she told the BBC."It's similar to having a crush on a TV star, but even further removed from cheating since there is no other actual person involved.”After Franco posted a video on the subject, hundreds of commenters appeared to agree with her, although some did have reservations."To be honest, it depends," wrote one. "If you're cancelling plans with your significant other or directing your intimacy towards a fictional character, then that is a little odd."Image source, Rockstar gamesImage caption, Rockstar has said players do not have to build a romantic connection in the gameMimicking social relationshipsFor decades, video games have allowed players to build relationships with non-player characters, or NPCs.Gamers could marry villagers in Harvest Moon in 1996, shape emotional storylines in Final Fantasy VII and pursue more complex romances in role-playing games like Baldur's Gate II.In life simulator The Sims, they could flirt, date, marry and have children with computer-controlled characters.But all those interactions were tightly scripted, based on rules and storylines written in advance by game developers.GTA 6 appears to offer something more dynamic, allowing players to shape the relationship between Jason and Lucia through a wider range of open-world interactions and choices."The more sophisticated games get, the less likely it is that players get pulled out of the experience," says Arienne Ferchaud, an associate professor at Florida State University who studies how people form connections with fictional characters."Games are doing a better job of mimicking reality and mimicking social relationships."Figure caption, Can you cheat on your partner in a video game character?Grand Theft Auto 6 may represent the current cutting edge of game design, but the next leap forward could come from artificial intelligence.Nvidia, Ubisoft and other huge tech companies are already experimenting with generative AI systems that allow players to hold more natural conversations with NPCs.Future characters could remember past encounters, react to a player's actions and build relationships that change over time rather than following a pre-written script.Ferchaud believes that could make games feel even more immersive."You could have relationships that feel more solid or more special," she says, although she argues AI as it exists today would still be creating "a stronger illusion" rather than a genuinely meaningful connection.Whether that is exciting or unsettling may depend on the player, and there has been some resistance to the wider use of the technology in gaming.Franco says she is already seeing adverts for AI chatbots that let fans talk to their favourite anime characters."I can definitely see AI integrating into games and making it a more realistic experience," she says. "But should that happen I would still see it as just a game. At the end of the day you can't cheat with lines of code."

schema.headline: GTA 6: Can you cheat on someone with a video game character?

title: A wave of homemade, synthetic drugs sweeps US and deepens crisis
description: Figure caption, The BBC’s Quentin Sommerville joins officers at Cook County as they carry out an early morning raidBy Quentin SommervilleInternational
body: Figure caption, The BBC’s Quentin Sommerville joins officers at Cook County as they carry out an early morning raidBy Quentin SommervilleInternational correspondent, Columbus, OhioWarning: This story contains descriptions of drug-taking from the start and discusses suicideThe few grains of fentanyl sit in the silver foil as a straw, held between Mike's lips, hovers above, with a cigarette lighter below. The 48-year-old army veteran is crouched low in an alleyway in Columbus, Ohio's Linden neighbourhood."This drug will damn near make you do anything, unfortunately," he says.The hit he's smoking cost three or four dollars."You can snort too much and you can't take it back. Kind of like a gunshot. Can't call the bullet back," he says.He burns the foil and inhales. As the opioid takes hold, he grips the fence behind him. He sways as a low moan comes from deep in his throat - he could be humming a tune.We've spent a few days with Mike - he's been our guide through the neighbourhood's back streets. Everyone seems to know him and he's regarded fondly. He helps out at a local pawn shop and gas station, and that's how he feeds his 20-year-old opioid addiction.Synthetic opioids are more powerful and in plentiful supply, and they have transformed the drugs landscape. Fentanyl, which is entirely man-made, is 50 to 100 times more powerful than heroin, which is cultivated from poppies. It is now often cut with synthetic tranquillisers, which make reviving overdose victims more difficult. These are homemade threats, where cocktails of synthetics can be made in American basements and bathtubs.America's War on Drugs: The Synthetic WaveExtraordinary access shows how strong synthetic drugs are changing America's drug crisis.Image source, Darren Conway/BBCImage caption, "This drug will damn near make you do anything, unfortunately," says Mike as he lights up a few grains of fentanylImage source, Darren Conway/BBCImage caption, Mike, a former army veteran, acts as our guide through the neighbourhood's back streets We have Naloxone (brand name Narcan) in our pockets, in case anyone on our team comes into contact with fentanyl or anyone around us overdoses. It's a nasal spray that immediately reverses opioid overdoses and its widespread adoption has transformed the number of fatal overdoses in the United States.At its peak in 2022, 110,000 Americans were dying from overdoses, mostly from opioids. The number has been dropping since, down to around 70,000 last year. But that doesn't mean the opioid crisis is over.It's likely that the reversal drug in my pocket, which has saved tens of thousands of drug users' lives, would not have worked on Mike. Because he wasn't just smoking fentanyl.The pupils in his milky blue eyes shrink to pin pricks. "Opioids make your pupils go smaller, but not that small," he says in a singsong voice. Even the fentanyl, dangerous enough on its own, has other synthetics added.When we ask what he thinks his drugs have been cut with, he replies: "Xylazine, and the one we can't pronounce."Medetomidine is what he means. Like xyalzine, it is also referred to as tranq and both are synthetic animal tranquilisers. "Large animal tranquilisers," as one recovery expert told me.They help prolong the high from the fentanyl but are a sedative that slows breathing and, importantly, naloxone doesn't work against them. Xylazine also causes necrotic skin ulcers, wounds so deep they can make it down to the bone and are difficult to treat.Recovery group offering hopeAt the Glenwood Church on the other side of town, members of the Hope Dealer Community, a recovery group, gather for a weekly meeting. For many, their struggles are written in their care-worn faces, and their eyes are those of survivors of a great trauma.They take to the stage at the front of the church and share their stories with a brutal and courageous honesty.One man tells the story of his overdose in July 2022. Two paramedics worked on him, trying to save his life. He had naloxone drips in both arms. They hit him with the opioid reversal three times to no avail. "That's it, I'm gonna call it," said one of the medics. But the other insisted on one more try, and it was that which saved his life.As the crowd shouts encouragement, Tonya takes to the lectern. She recounts how her nephew died of an overdose while she was overdosing at the same time from crack cocaine, a stimulant spiked with fentanyl, a synthetic opioid."It's not luck. I'm supposed to be here," she says with tears in her eyes. The audience yells its agreement.Image source, Darren Conway/BBCImage caption, Members of the Hope Dealer Community, a recovery group, gather for a weekly meeting at Glenwood ChurchImage source, Darren Conway/BBCImage caption, One of those gathered at the church, Tonya, recounts how her nephew died of an overdose while she was overdosing at the same timeBoth in Columbus, and later in Chicago, we would hear of crack cocaine users who had died of overdoses after their drugs contained fentanyl. On the street, it's called a "hot dose"."In the last 12 months in Franklin County [Columbus], 78% of fatal overdoses are from stimulants," explains Scott Sanders, 65, who runs Hope Dealers.Scott is almost 10 years sober, a powerfully built man in his early 60s with an electric energy. When he asks the room to raise their hands if anyone has overdosed, most of the gathering does so."The crisis has just shifted," Scott tells me afterwards. "The tragedy is stimulant users who are purchasing crack think that's what they're getting, and they're not. They're getting crack mixed with fentanyl or other opioid cocktails and overdosing without being aware of it."Image source, Darren Conway/BBCImage caption, Scott Sanders, 65, is almost 10 years sober and runs Hope DealersOverdose deaths among black men in Ohio are actually increasing, he adds.His organisation works with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) on a drug sampling programme. Participants bring their needles or pipes for swabbing and the samples are sent to the CDC's laboratory in North Carolina.That's how we learned that Mike's instincts were right, he likely wasn't just smoking fentanyl. One of the drug kits he brought in tested positive for medetomidine."The drug supply in 2026 is this: we think we are buying crack but we're not, we're buying a number of different things," says Scott. "Today it is mixed, not just cut, but mixed with other drugs such as fentanyl or meth, and then other adulterants chemicals that are made in basements."And it was basement-made synthetic drugs that would cause a dramatic increase in overdose deaths one state over, in Illinois.Watch the documentary on YouTube, externalI meet a dealer in Chicago who works for the Mexican cartels selling fentanyl. He would only speak to us if we agreed to mask his identity.Challenged on his role in the 50,000 people dying each year because of the opioid crisis, he says he knows it is wrong. But when asked why he keeps doing it, he said the end justifies the means.He told me that despite the latest efforts by the US government to target the cartels by declaring them terrorist groups and labelling fentanyl a weapon of mass destruction, his supply chain is as strong as ever.When I ask him if the targeting of boats containing suspected traffickers by the Trump administration has made any difference, he replies that his product is still getting through from Mexico. "If it doesn't go over the wall, it goes under the wall. If it doesn't go through the border, it comes through the top border. This game is about adaptability."And when I asked what has changed in his business, his answer was clear.  "Synthetics. We haven't seen... what synthetics can do yet. It's not even the tip of the iceberg," he tells me.A novel approach Chicago's largest jail, one of the largest jails in America, is Cook County. Traditional drugs were usually brought into the jail in body cavities, so the jail had the same body scanners you find at airports to prevent that happening."In 2023, all of a sudden we saw a spike in overdose deaths, but then hand in hand with that we saw, around persons that had either passed away or people we revived, paper all over the place," explains Sheriff Tom Dart, who runs the jail. "We were seeing paper that was being burned and all of this was completely novel."The facility, which averages one or two overdose deaths a year, lost eight inmates that year to fatal seizures.Security footage shows prisoners spasming and collapsing. It also showed them lighting paper in microwaves in the cell block kitchens.It was indeed, as Dart said, a novel approach. Drugs were being mailed into the jail soaked in the pages of books and in letters."Cannabinoids and being soaked in a range of other things that were then subsequently lit on fire and inhaled to get high", the sheriff explained.Cannabinoids, sometimes know as K2, are an entirely synthetic version of a cannabis plant extract. They are extremely dangerous and were to blame for the fatal seizures.Image source, Darren Conway/BBCImage caption, In Chicago's largest jail, drugs were soaked in the pages of books and in lettersIn August, I joined Dart's corrections officers as they prepared for an early morning raid on the jail's high security D block. Around two dozen officers tread lightly and speak in hushed tones as they gather outside the block door. "Don't let them hear you. Silence, silence," commands one of the officers leading the search.As the officers rush in, I smell burning paper in the air and can hear the sound of toilets flushing, presumably as contraband is hurriedly disposed of.As the search gets under way, the focus is on any paper in the cells - the books and letters belonging to inmates.The detainees are escorted to a holding area as the cells are turned over. Every scrap of paper in the rooms is checked by the officers. There are burn marks on the vents in many of the cells, where inmates place smoulder tapers that allow them to ignite the drug-soaked paper.Now every piece of post that enters the jail is scanned for moisture. Somewhere between a quarter and a fifth of all packages and letters test positive and are rejected.Image source, Darren Conway/BBCImage caption, Between a quarter and a fifth of all packages and letters that enter the jail test positive for moistureOutside the jail's walls, it's not hard to encounter the effects of the synthetic drugs wave on Chicago's streets. In the west of the city, day and night, men and women are bent double, swaying, as Mike did, as fentanyl and other synthetics surge through them.In the upscale Oak Park neighbourhood, the local metro station has a vending machine that dispenses naloxone for free. Nearby, a gaunt-looking man in a wheelchair has deep wounds in his legs, likely from xylazine use. He's being tended to by 40-year-old Karen Bell.Karen is a recovery worker with the group Liv4Lali. A former heroin user, she's 17 years free from hard drugs.She exudes kindness, and when I ask her about the drugs being used now, she says, "so many things are being mixed in right now. And it's affecting our bodies, whether it's the wounds, whether it's the withdrawals - and sometimes wounds can extend to the point where it's life changing."Her organisation, like Hope Dealers in Columbus, distributes test strips which check drugs for fentanyl, medetomidine, xylazine and other adulterants.The drugs now, says Karen, are "way more dangerous"."Because before, back in my day, I stopped using heroin 17 years ago, right. That was still heroin. When you bought that you knew it was heroin. But now, when you buy a bag, you don't know really what it is," she tells me.Image source, Darren Conway/BBCImage caption, Karen, a recovery worker, tends to a gaunt-looking man in a wheelchair in an upscale part of town Dart has been sheriff of Cook County for 20 years, so I ask him how the war on drugs was progressing. "I don't think there's anybody involved with it who would sit there and say it's a raging success. It's not," he tells me. And the new problem, he says, reiterating the Chicago drug dealer, is synthetics."The tradition has always been that law enforcement had an even more vital role because everything that was potent was coming across the border, whether it was coming from Colombia, Mexico, China, the poppy fields of Afghanistan. Now, with the explosion of synthetic drugs, people can do this in their house, in their sink, in their bathtub, you name it."Victory in the war on drugs won't come from focusing just on the supply side, the sheriff adds. "Front and centre there's got to be huge substance abuse treatment," he says, mentioning a number of recovery programmes running in his jail. "You can reduce the market if you can address people's issues with substance abuse. And I know many people who, after long struggles, have come out on the other side in a really good way."'A lot of people are struggling'Karen knows how difficult it is to quit. She was still using heroin when she got pregnant with her daughter, Abby, now 17. After our meeting at the metro station, I meet them both in a country park in a suburb outside Chicago. With typical care, Karen tells me to watch out for the poison ivy as we walk along a muddy track.It wasn't far from here, around 17 years ago, that she was at her lowest ebb.Image source, Darren Conway/BBCImage caption, Karen says her pregnancy was an opportunity to get clean. She's 17 years free from hard drugs As the wind blows through a tall oak tree beside us, she says: "The day I found out I was pregnant, I was on my way to commit suicide. I was so fed up with trying to quit. I was so fed up with living in a tent in the woods, using a bucket. I was so fed up with losing my friends and family because I was just so ashamed."A pregnancy test changed her mind. She then spent time in Cook County jail for theft. Her parents, sensing an opportunity for her to get clean, refused to pay her bail money. So Karen got clean and Abby was born inside the jail.When I ask Abby, who wants to become a tattoo artist, whether she's ever been tempted to experiment with drugs, she says: "Nah, I've seen it mess with my family too much, with my dad, my mum, killing my aunt, my uncles. You know, it's not worth it to get high for like a couple of hours."She continues: "There's a lot of people are struggling, especially that our country is raising our prices, raising the prices on food and it's causing it. A lot of mental health now is very expensive so people can't get help, and one way they can turn to that is by drugs."Generations of Americans have endured the drugs crisis, but it is never the same crisis. It has shifted from heroin, to prescription opioids to fentanyl and now to a whole new range of synthetics.Successive administrations have fought - and lost - the war against drugs. The dealers, the suppliers, the cartels and users all adapt, always a few steps ahead of efforts to stop them.Additional reporting by Darren ConwayIf you are suffering distress or despair and need support, you could speak to a health professional, or an organisation that offers support. Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide, external.A list of UK organisations that can help is available here.

schema.headline: A wave of homemade, synthetic drugs sweeps US and deepens crisis

title: Search for Amelia Earhart's plane resumes after stormy weather
description: Image source, Purdue UniversityImage caption, Sirisha Bandla (right), pictured with expedition lead Steve Schultz, said the crew was "really excited"B
body: Image source, Purdue UniversityImage caption, Sirisha Bandla (right), pictured with expedition lead Steve Schultz, said the crew was "really excited"ByAleks PhillipsA search for the wreckage of Amelia Earhart's plane on a remote island in the Pacific Ocean has resumed after severe weather caused researchers to stop for several days.A team has travelled to Nikumaroro Island, part of Kiribati, hoping to solve the mystery of the famed aviator's disappearance by investigating the so-called Taraia Object, spotted in the atoll's lagoon in aerial imagery.The American pioneer vanished while attempting to circumnavigate the globe in 1937, spawning decades of speculation about her fate.Rough seas and strong winds forced the team to remain on their research vessel for three days, until the weather cleared on Sunday."We are finally getting off the ship and able to land on Nikumaroro," Sirisha Bandla, a technology specialist who is part of the expedition, said in a video update from the deck of the Marin Mainiku.The researchers arrived at the uninhabited atoll last week and began an underwater survey of the area of interest. But the weather - powered by strong El Niño conditions in the Pacific - has so far prevented them from beginning a second of three phases, in which underwater objects will be probed to determine their depth and sediment will be dredged.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Amelia Earhart disappeared over the Pacific Ocean while piloting her Electra plane in 1937"We're working to get everything done today if we can," Bandla said. "The crew's really excited."Earhart had already successfully flown from California across South America, Africa and Asia in her twin-engine Lockheed Electra when she arrived in Lae, Papua New Guinea on 2 July 1937.From there, she and her navigator Fred Noonan had planned to travel towards Hawaii and then finally back to California.But her plane vanished without a trace while trying to reach Howland Island, a remote, uninhabited coral island near Nikumaroro, to refuel.One theory is that Earhart unintentionally navigated to Nikumaroro, where she ditched her plane and died a castaway.Images of the so-called Taraia Object - which Purdue University says is visible in photography dating back to 1938 - show what could be the remnants of a small aircraft sitting in shallow waters, though other explorers remain sceptical.Image source, Archaeological Legacy InstituteImage caption, A satellite image of the so-called Taraia Object in a lagoon on NikumaroroInterest in the expedition prompted New Zealand's Air Force Museum to publish, external previously unseen reconnaissance images of Nikumaroro on Friday.While the Taraia Object is not obviously visible in any of the black-and-white slides, taken in 1938 from a seaplane, they do show the beached wreck of the SS Norwich City, a British merchant vessel that ran aground on the island during a storm in 1929, killing 11.Purdue, which with the US-based Archaeological Legacy Institute (ALI) is spearheading the expedition, said the incident demonstrated the risks surrounding the island.To get into the atoll's lagoon, a boat has to navigate through a narrow gap created in the reef by the British in 1963 - the last time the island was inhabited.But the university said wind gusts of up to 27 knots (31mph) present around the island until Sunday meant the transport boat could be knocked into the reef by crashing waves.Image source, RNZAFImage caption, Images from 1938 released by the Air Force Museum of New Zealand this week show Nikumaroro - then Gardner Island - with the SS Norwich City wreck in the bottom right cornerHowever, it said the Norwich City wreck may lend credence to the researchers' theory. Purdue said a 15-year-old in Florida reported hearing Earhart's voice repeating "New York City" over her father's shortwave radio shortly after the aviator vanished. Proponents of the castaway theory argue this may have been a misunderstanding of Earhart giving her location as near the Norwich City.As a result of the three-day hold, the research team has extended the expedition time to complete its fieldwork and has yet to indicate whether they had found any promising evidence of Earhart's plane.ALI director Rick Pettigrew said the team was aware of the global interest in the expedition and would share its results "as soon as we are able". Purdue suggested before the poor weather hit that it could identify the Taraia Object in a matter of days.While researchers have previously found evidence of a human presence on the island around the time of Earhart's disappearance, some skeptics believe the Taraia Object was just a tree that had fallen from the atoll into the lagoon.Previous attempts to find her Electra have also come up short.In 2024, a group of researchers said they may have found it lying around 4,877m (16,000ft) below the surface near Howland Island through sonar imaging - but this was later confirmed to be a rock formation.Similarly, an expedition in 2019 to investigate a photograph of what might have been landing gear protruding from the water near Nikumaroro also failed to find anything.

title: Champions Cup: Northampton Saints 28-12 Cardiff - Prem club wins Champions Cup opener
description: Investec Champions CupNorthampton (14) 28Tries: Pater, Thame, Hendy, Dingwall Cons: Belleau 3, PaterCardiff (0) 12Tries: Millard, Grady Con: EvansNort
body: Investec Champions CupNorthampton (14) 28Tries: Pater, Thame, Hendy, Dingwall Cons: Belleau 3, PaterCardiff (0) 12Tries: Millard, Grady Con: EvansNorthampton became the only English side to win in the opening round of the Champions Cup by battling past Cardiff.Saints, quarter-finalists last season, scored four tries at Franklin's Gardens in a nervy Pool Four encounter.The English champions led 14-0 at half-time thanks to efforts in tricky conditions by James Pater and Toby Thame.Tenacious Cardiff struck back through Harri Millard and Mason Grady to make it a two-point game in the final quarter.But George Hendy and Fraser Dingwall responded as Northampton got off to a winning start, albeit without a bonus point.Northampton's success came at the end of a chastening opening weekend of the top-tier tournament for Prem clubs, with Gloucester drawing against champions Bordeaux-Begles but six other sides losing.Cardiff's return to the top tier of Europe after two seasons in the Challenge Cup was a considerable one.Saints had scored 24 tries in their three opening fixtures of their Prem title defence, including 11 against Bath last time out at Franklin's Gardens.The Welsh side also had to contend with a five-day turnaround to a United Rugby Championship (URC) fixture against Sharks at Cardiff Arms Park.That led to several influential players being held back, although they did give first appearances of the season to Wales and Lions internationals Taulupe Faletau and Josh Adams after injury.Northampton also made changes because of a big fixture on the horizon - the short trip to Leicester on Saturday - but got the job done.Full-back Pater opened the scoring for Saints with a supporting run and centre Thame crashed over after 20 minutes.Both Northampton number eight Callum Chick and Cardiff lock Tom Manz knocked on going for the line as slippery conditions led to it being 14-0 at half-time.The Blue and Blacks struck back early in the second half when centre Millard hit a nice line in the 22 and then defended stoutly to frustrate their hosts, forcing them into a raft of handling errors.It was 14-12 on the hour when, after Saints fly-half Anthony Belleau was sin-binned for a breakdown offence, the ball was floated to the right by Jarrod Evans for Grady to cross.Cardiff scented an upset only for Hendy to respond swiftly, juggling the ball for a try that Pater converted.The Northampton wing went from scoring five points to saving them by chasing down Adams when a try seemed certain.Dingwall dashed over in the 78th minute but the hosts could not find the fifth try that was needed for a five-point haul.Northampton: Pater; Sleightholme, Hutchinson, Thame, Hendy; Belleau, Mitchell; Fischetti, Smith, Kundiona, Lockett, van der Mescht, Kemeny, Taylor, Chick.Replacements: Langdon, Els, Neculai, Prowse, Ulcoq, McParland, Smith, Dingwall.Yellow card: Belleau 60.Cardiff: Young; Grady, Millard, Emanuel, Bowen; Evans, Mulder; Southworth, D Hughes (capt), Wainwright, Manz, Thornton, Paea, D Thomas, Faletau.Replacements: E Lloyd, Barratt, Cowell, McNally, De La Rua, S Davies, Sheedy, Adams.Referee: Jeremy Rozier (France)Assistant referees: Thomas Charabas (France) & Cyrille Boulay (France)TMO: Julien Castaignede (France)
